verses.1: Al-Mizan explains that tanzīl, though formally a verbal noun, means the Book that has been sent down; its attachment to “the Book” gives it this adjectival sense. Calling it from the Lord of all the worlds introduces the sūrah’s affirmations of monotheism and resurrection against idolaters who denied a single Lord of all worlds, assigning each world its own deity and treating God as the deity of those deities.

verses.3:
Al-Mizan takes “Or” as disjunctive: the deniers claim that the Prophet fabricated the Qur’an and falsely ascribed it to God, while God answers that it is the truth from their Lord, sent so that he may warn and guide a people without a previous warner.

Some commentators identify these people as Quraysh, unlike Arab tribes said in narrations to have received prophets. Others refer to the interval between Jesus and Muḥammad. The commentary rejects the idea that this interval contained absolutely no prophets; it means only that no prophet came with a new law or scripture. The hoped-for guidance is the purpose of sending the Messenger, but tarajjī belongs to the situation or the people addressed, not to God Himself.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan explains “settling upon the Throne” (istawāʾ ʿalā al-ʿarsh) as a visual allusion to God’s direction of all existents through the comprehensive natural order governing the cosmos. Its mention after creation establishes not creation alone but God’s exclusive lordship and divinity. Idolaters acknowledged God as sole Creator, yet assigned cosmic governance, worship, and intercession to their lesser deities. Since the originator of things must also direct their affairs, creation and governance are inseparable: the sole Creator is also the sole Lord and object of worship.

Guardianship and intercession belong to governance. A walī directs a thing’s affairs; because the universal and particular orders on which life depends follow from creation, God alone is the guardian of all things. A shafīʿ completes a deficient cause so that it produces its effect. Created causes consist of cooperating elements, which in this sense intercede for one another; but since God originates the causes, their elements, and their connections, He alone is their true and ultimate intercessor.

The commentary further explains that the Beautiful Names mediate the divine effusion to creation. A thing’s existence is realized through several Names, with more specific Names mediating between it and more general ones. Thus God may be called an intercessor in the sense that His attributes intercede with other attributes on behalf of a thing: one seeks refuge from His wrath in His mercy and from His justice in His grace. But God’s interceding with someone other than Himself is impossible.

Al-Mizan rejects attempts to evade the proper meaning of shafīʿ. Reading dūnahu as “with Him,” with an added sense of disregarding God, conflicts with min, which requires “other than,” and lacks textual basis. Taking shafīʿ metaphorically as “helper” is needless. Treating intercession as merely an argument addressed on idolaters’ own terms does not preserve the verse’s direct sense. Reading dūnahu as “with” and making its pronoun refer to divine punishment is likewise arbitrary. The closing question rebukes those who ignore the rational evidence that all governance belongs to God and therefore wrongly claim other guardians or intercessors.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan holds that amr here means “affair” (shaʾn), not a command opposed to prohibition: God directs the affairs of all beings. Tadbīr is the successive ordering of one affair after another, so phenomena come to be in a chain extending from heaven to earth according to measure. The subsequent ascent suggests that this direction includes a staged descent from heaven to earth.

Because the affair descends from the heavens and then returns to God by the same route, “heavens” apparently denotes the station of divine proximity and presence from which all affairs issue and to which decisive matters return, not the physical sky. It may alternatively denote the centre from which earthly affairs are directed, while God encompasses all things; the commentary finds this latter reading easier to understand.

The thousand-year day is a period which, if measured by terrestrial motion and time, would equal a thousand human years; earthly days, months, and years do not delimit the realm of divine proximity. Although the verse admits questions over whether this duration includes descent, ascent, earthly stay, all phenomena, or the Resurrection, Al-Mizan judges it most reasonable that “in a day” qualifies only the ascent and denotes one of the fifty stages of the Day of Resurrection. And God knows best.
verses.6: Al-Mizan states that the vocabulary of the verse has already been explained and that the relevance of its three Divine Names is clear from the context.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan, citing al-Rāghib, explains ḥasan as what is pleasant or desirable to reason, desire, or the senses. A thing is ḥasan when its parts are harmonious and its whole suits its end. Every created thing is therefore internally harmonious and equipped for its perfection and felicity in the best form appropriate to its purpose.

Perceived evil has no independent created reality. It is either privation (dhā ʿunwān ʿadamī), the absence of what ought to be present—as injustice deprives someone of a right and zinā violates divine law and harms society—or it is relative to another thing and human disposition. The latter kind ultimately returns to privation. Since God creates all things and perfects everything He creates, creation (khulqah) entails perfection (ḥusn): nothing existing is evil insofar as it exists, and sins and evil deeds are not created as evil in an absolute sense.

“Man” denotes the human species. Its creation began from clay because humanity descends from Adam and Eve, who were created from clay without sexual reproduction. The following mention of progeny from a base fluid distinguishes ordinary procreation from that original creation; otherwise the wording would have said that He made him, rather than his progeny, from such fluid.
verses.8: Al-Mizan, following Majmaʿ al-Bayān, explains sulālah as an extract or quintessence, and calls semen an extract because it is drawn from the loins. Mahīn means lowly or weak, while thumma indicates an interval. The verse thus means that human offspring are subsequently born through procreation from an extract of lowly, weak fluid.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan explains taswiyah as shaping or completing a thing. God’s breathing into man of His Spirit is a metaphor, and the possessive expression magnifies the spirit’s rank rather than making it a part of God. Thus, after shaping the human being whose creation began from clay and whose progeny come through base fluid, God breathed into him of the noble spirit belonging to Him.

Hearing and sight are sensory faculties, while hearts are cognitive faculties more general than imagination or reason. “Little do you thank” reproaches people for their scant gratitude, whether read as an aside or as qualifying God’s bestowal of these faculties. The shift from third-person description to direct address stresses that God’s blessings encompass creatures and exceed their thanks: none can fully thank Him, and many are especially ungrateful.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan reads “lost in the dust” as complete dissipation or disappearance after death: bodies have disintegrated into the earth so thoroughly that no trace or memory remains. The question about being created anew is rhetorical and denies the possibility of the Resurrection.

The commentary says their real denial is not based on a denial of God’s power to create anew, but on their refusal to believe that they will return to and encounter their Lord. The Qur’an therefore answers by demonstrating that they will in fact return to Him.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan explains tawaffī as taking something completely. The angel of death is charged with people in a sense broader than merely causing death and taking souls. The Qur’an can ascribe this taking to messenger angels, to the angel of death, or to God because these are distinct levels of one causal order: assistant angels are the immediate agents, the angel of death directs them by God’s command, and God is the ultimate cause encompassing them all.

The return to the Lord is the encounter at the Resurrection, occurring after the taking away, as thumma indicates. This answers the objection that resurrection is impossible once bodies are dispersed in the earth. The angel of death takes the person fully from the body by severing the soul’s bond with it. The soul is the true “I,” preserved from loss even while the body changes and disintegrates; at resurrection it returns to the body for judgment and recompense.

The verse consequently teaches that human individuality belongs to the soul, not to the body or one of its states. The soul neither disintegrates nor ceases at death, but remains preserved in God’s power until its return. Interpreting “taken away” as death in a merely general sense obscures this answer and leads to strained explanations of its connection with the preceding objection.
verses.12:
Al-Mizan identifies “the guilty” (mujrimīn) as the particular people who denied the Resurrection. Their standing “before their Lord” is the encounter with Him that they formerly denied. On that day they lower their heads in shame, humiliation, and regret, confessing that they have seen and heard, and ask to return to the world to perform righteous deeds.

They have then gained complete certainty of faith, but possess no righteous deeds to accompany it and secure salvation. Though they will acknowledge what they now deny and ask to be sent back, they will not be returned.
verses.13:
Al-Mizan explains that, had God wished, He could have given every person the guidance needed through each person’s own free choice, just as believers are guided by their free choice. Compulsion would make moral obligation and final recompense pointless.

But God’s prior word became due: He would fill hell with jinn and humans. This is the decree concerning Iblīs and those who follow him, who are destined for everlasting punishment. God does not guide them because of the wrongdoing and transgression by which they abandoned servanthood (ʿubūdiyyah).
verses.14:
Al-Mizan explains nisyān here not as the loss of an image from memory, but as neglecting something important. Because the followers of Iblīs stubbornly ignored and denied the encounter of this Day, failing to act righteously for its reward, they are told to taste punishment; on that Day God will pay no heed to their happiness or salvation.

“Taste the everlasting punishment because of what you used to do” emphasizes that the punishment is everlasting and that their neglect of the Day consisted in their evil deeds.
verses.15: Al-Mizan explains that true īmān is confined to those ready for genuine belief: when reminded of God’s signs, which establish His exclusive lordship and divinity and entail the Resurrection and the prophetic summons to faith and good works, they submit to the truth. Their prostration expresses humility and obedience before God, while their praise declares Him transcendent above creation and glorifies Him. Though these are outward acts, they manifest the inward absence of arrogance toward God’s lordship and divinity.
verses.16: Al-Mizan says that this verse describes the believers’ actions. Their sides “vacate” their beds because they forgo sleep to supplicate in the night, when most people sleep; this includes the supererogatory night prayers. They pray with both fear and hope: neither fear that despairs of divine mercy nor hope that feels secure from God’s anger and devising, but the proper etiquette of servanthood guided by God. They also spend, in God’s way, from what He has provided them.
verses.17: Al-Mizan explains that this promised reward follows from the believers’ qualities and deeds. The indefinite nafs under negation means that no soul at all can know or imagine the hidden comfort (qurrat aʿyun) God has stored for them. By relating this comfort to “eyes” rather than to their particular eyes, the verse indicates a comfort for whoever has eyes, bestowed as recompense for their worldly deeds.
verses.18: Al-Mizan defines īmān as the soul’s settling upon what it knows, a state whose necessary consequence is to act upon that faith. Fisq is its opposite: the sinner departs from obedience to God, as a date splits out of its skin. The verse’s question is rhetorical and demands denial of any equality between the faithful and the transgressor; its closing statement emphatically confirms that they are not alike.
verses.19: Al-Mizan explains that the faithful who do righteous deeds receive gardens as their maʾwā, an abode where one takes shelter and rests. These gardens are their nuzul: originally the food and drink prepared for a guest, and also used for a gift generally, granted in return for their deeds.
verses.20: Al-Mizan explains that the Fire is the transgressors’ “refuge” in the sense that they have no escape from it: whenever they try to leave, they are returned. The transgressors are the deniers of the Resurrection, and their command to taste the Fire they denied shames them in return for their having shamed the faithful in this world for believing in the Resurrection.
verses.21: Al-Mizan holds that, because the purpose of the nearer punishment is to bring its recipients back to God through repentance, it is punishment suffered in this world to frighten and warn them, not destructive punishment in this world or punishment after death. It may take forms such as scarcity, illness, and killing, and is meant to lead them to repent of polytheism and obstinacy before the greater punishment of the Day of Resurrection. It is called the “nearer,” rather than the “least,” punishment, and the Hereafter’s punishment the “greater,” rather than the “furthest,” because the context is one of threat.
verses.22: Al-Mizan treats the verse as the rationale for the greater punishment. Those who turn away after being reminded of their Lord’s signs are the gravest wrongdoers and thus guilty. God’s vengeance upon the guilty is therefore their punishment, and it is God Himself who exacts that vengeance.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan identifies the Book as the Torah. It regards the interpretations that make “his encounter” an encounter with Moses—whether during the Night Journey or on the Day of Resurrection—an encounter of Moses with the Book, the Prophet’s encounter with the Book, or a prediction that the Prophet will suffer Moses’ persecution, as fundamentally unsound because they do not explain the verse’s relation to what precedes it.

It is possible—and God knows best—that the pronoun refers to God and the encounter to the Resurrection, when all will stand before their Lord without a barrier; this accords with the earlier description of the Resurrection as an “encounter” (liqāʾ). It is also possible that it denotes the Prophet’s attention being wholly absorbed by God during Qur’anic revelation, as indicated by some narrations; the verse’s ending appears to support this latter reading more strongly. The Torah was made a guidance, that is, a guide, for the Children of Israel.
verses.24: Al-Mizan explains that God appointed imāms from among the Children of Israel to guide by His command only after they had remained steadfast in their religion and attained certainty in His signs. The Torah was thus a mercy and source of blessing in two respects: it guided those who followed it to the truth, and it nurtured those chosen as imāms, who in turn guided others by God’s command.
verses.25: Al-Mizan explains that the differences in question are religious differences that arose from enmity among the Children of Israel after knowledge had come to them. On the Day of Resurrection, God will judge between them by separating truth from falsehood and the people of truth from the people of falsehood.
verses.26: Al-Mizan explains a wa lam yahdi lahum as asking whether it has not become clear to them how many earlier generations God destroyed, even though they walk among those generations’ dwellings. The destroyed generations are the subject of yahdi, whose construction conveys becoming clear to them. The ruins are signs, and the call to “listen” means to heed the admonition, thereby accepting and obeying the truth.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan, citing Majmaʿ al-Bayān, explains that sūq is to drive something along a route and that al-arḍ al-juzur is land made barren by lack of rain. Zarʿ, though literally a verbal noun for sowing, here means the crops produced. Driving water to such land means driving rain-bearing clouds to it; rain revives the earth, brings forth plants, and feeds people and their domesticated cattle. This is a sign of God’s beneficent governance of living creation.

The closing question both exhorts and reproaches them to see. It invokes sight, unlike the preceding verse’s invocation of hearing, because the destruction of earlier peoples is known through transmitted reports, whereas the movement of water to barren land, the growth of plants, and their consumption by humans and animals are directly seen.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan explains fatḥ as unbarring or removing an obstacle; regarding an issue, it means settling it and removing its impediment, hence judgement. Here it may refer either to judgement on the Day of Resurrection or to making the idolaters taste the nearer punishment, or taking vengeance on them, in this world. Some commentators therefore take it as the Resurrection, while others identify it with the Battle of Badr or the conquest of Mecca.

The latter identifications do not fit the reply that faith will not benefit the faithless on the day of judgement and that they will receive no respite, unless their subsequent profession of faith was merely hypocrisy (nifāq): a compelled outward show that never entered their hearts. Fatḥ could also mean God’s judgement between the Prophet and the Muslim ummah in the End Times. In every case, the answer rebukes the idolaters’ impatience by declaring a judgement after which disbelief can no longer be remedied by faith and none will be spared punishment or granted respite.

verses.30: Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is commanded to disregard them and await God’s judgement, while they await his death or killing in hopes that his mission will fail. He is to wait for God to grant truth and its people victory over falsehood and its people. The context therefore shows that this fatḥ is an event in this world, not the Hereafter.
